speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, as the house knows the Columbia river treaty was signed in Washington yesterday. The President and Secretary of State and the under secretary of the interior signed for the United States of America. The treaty was signed for Canada by myself together with the Minister of Justice and the Canadian ambassador at Washington.
I indicated the other day that I would table at the earliest possible date copies of the treaty and also the statement I made outlining some of the features and particulars of that treaty. In view of the widespread interest in these documents I propose that with the consent of the house they be printed as an appendix to Hansard.
May I say that in the signing of this tremendous treaty the course followed was one that gave emphasis to the importance of the occasion. The fact is that it was the last major official discharge of responsibility on the part of the President of the United States. That fact gives it emphasis. During the course of our stay there the Minister of Justice, myself and several representatives from the two countries were entertained at luncheon at the White House, the last function of the kind that will take place during the presidency of Dwight D. Eisenhower.
I agree with the remarks that were made at the conclusion of this treaty, that it represents a major advance in co-operation by the two nations without the sacrifice of the rights, the sovereignty or otherwise of either
country, and is indeed a landmark in responsible joint action by nations for their economic betterment.
With the leave of the house, as I indicated earlier, I therefore wish to table the treaty in both English and French, and the summary in both languages.

1.	Did the Department of Public Works give consideration to a special arrangement with Raymond International on the lakehead terminal project which would have kept a work force on the job during January, February, and March, 1960?
2.	If so, how much extra was involved in terms of money, and how many men would have been kept on work during this period?

Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows:
1.	Yes.
2.	Had this proposal been accepted, an extra in addition to the regular cost would have

been approximately $41,000. From 40 to 60 men might have been employed for a ten week period.
3.	The proposal was not accepted partly because of the extra cost and chiefly by the fact that the pouring of concrete in adverse weather conditions gave us no assurance that it would carry the heavy loads which were involved. Even with extra precautions during January, February and March it would be extremely difficult to ensure proper heating of the aggregate and the protection and satisfactory curing of the concrete to provide proper strength in this exposed location.
It was decided it was better to press ahead with other major contracts at the lakehead to provide employment. Work has now started on one of these, a $3,953,185 contract which includes the construction of two large transit sheds, a number of other buildings, access roads, water and sewer and other services. Within a matter of weeks the number of men employed on this work will exceed those who would have been employed under the proposed arrangement. In addition a new contract will be awarded shortly for the Main street access bridge in the same development. Work is expected to start within a month and this will provide further employment.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
That a select committee, to be designated, be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure of this house for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business, with power to send for persons and papers, and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.

He said: Mr. Speaker, on January 18 last, on my suggestion, a committee of the house was set up under your chairmanship and direction which dealt with the rules, and changes were duly recommended in the report made on July 25, 1960. In that report the committee recommended that certain temporary orders of procedure be adopted on a trial basis effective only for the next session of parliament, the fourth session of the twenty fourth parliament. Those proposals are set out in detail in the report.
I think the experience of the last few weeks has been that the recommendations have been most beneficial. I think members in all parts of the house will agree that the recommendations were of such a nature and have proved to be so simple that they ought to receive consideration toward making them applicable not only to this session but to succeeding sessions. This, of course, is a matter for members in all parts of the house to determine.
There are various other matters which should be considered. Last year, on May 9, a motion to set up the committee was introduced by the Minister of Finance. At page 3687 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say that in the light of the length of time which was devoted to the study of the rules by the previous committee, I do not think the house will expect the committee to come forward with a final report at this session. If that should be the case, I am sure the house will be pleased to set up the committee again at the next following session to continue its work. The appointment at the present session, however, will at least launch the committee and enable it to carry forward its work. If the committee should see fit to make recommendations about changing the rules at this session, that matter will have to be considered however the report is received.
I believe-and I hope the house will agree -that this committee should be set up to carry on from where the committee of the last house concluded, to the end that the rules which are so necessary for the maintenance of efficient and expeditious debate should be viewed in greater detail than was possible at the last session. After all, rules are not like the laws of the Medes and the Persians. They should be reviewed regularly to the end that their effectiveness shall be tested and, if unsatisfactory in any way, be altered in the light of experience and circumstances.
I want to say a word to the members of the committee. I think the manner in which they came to agreement on recommendations at the last session, as in 1951, speaks highly of all members of the committee. No one wants to put parliament in a strait-jacket. No one wants to interfere with the fullest
Appointment of Committee on House Rules discussion. No one wants to bring about a denial of the rights of members to express themselves fully with the authority of the people they represent.
I think the experience has been, however, that the reduction in the length of speeches from 40 minutes to 30 minutes has improved the quality of speeches. After all, it is so much easier to make a speech of great length than a short and effective one. On one occasion Woodrow Wilson, I believe, was asked by Princeton University, of which he had been president for many years, whether he would accept an invitation to speak and how much notice he would require. I do not have before me the exact answer he gave and I am speaking from memory, but as I recall, his answer was that if he was to make a speech an hour long three or four days' notice would be ample, but if the speech was to be 10 or 15 minutes long he would require two or three months' notice.
While it is necessary on occasion, in order to elucidate a problem, to go beyond 30 or 40 minutes, in the normal range of debate nothing is more effective than a short, well reasoned and lucid argument. Quite an advance was made by the committee in that direction by reducing the period from 40 to 30 minutes, and I am sure that in consequence of that reduction no thought that the house should have had, no suggestion that would be beneficial, has been denied expression.
I therefore place this motion before the house hoping that it will receive unanimous approval.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are happy to support the motion for the setting up without delay of a committee to continue the work of a similar committee last session, which I think was effective and produced some constructive proposals under your own wise guidance. Anything that a committee of the house can do to recommend to the house procedures and proposals that will make our proceedings more businesslike should receive the support of all of us subject, of course, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, to the necessity of the fullest discussion of every measure before the house, something which is of particular concern to the opposition.
The Prime Minister mentioned one recommendation of the last committee reducing the length of speeches. In his view it has worked out very well. Perhaps it would not be appropriate for me to comment on that until the time comes when this process of improvement, if that is what it is, can be continued by putting the Prime Minister and myself under a similar time limit, which might make our speeches more effective also.

Appointment of Committee on House Rules
We support the motion and it is unnecessary for me to say anything more, as it would only delay the setting up of the committee. Therefore I merely express on behalf of our party our strong approval of the setting up of the committee. We hope it will continue its good work of last session in this field.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of being a member of the committee on procedure during the last session of the house and I feel, as other members do, that the committee was able to do effective work and made a report whose recommendations, up until this point during the present session, seem to be working well and in my opinion have made a contribution toward dealing with the business of the house during this session in a more effective way.
The members of the committee were generally agreed that any change in the rales should be first of all a temporary change on a trial basis and, second, should be agreed to unanimously by the members of the committee. So, Mr. Speaker, the whole question of the government using its majority to force the adoption of certain procedures did not arise. All the changes in the rules that are in effect during the present session were agreed to unanimously.
I think the changes have been good. There has been a reduction of two days in the time taken for the debate on the speech from the throne, and a reduction of two days also in the budget debate. There has been a general reduction in the length of speeches from 40 minutes to 30 minutes, with some particular exemptions. Authority has been given to the government to bring forward government measures in lieu of or by interrupting private members' days so that the government can get its legislative program before parliament and committees of the house can be set up. I think this has been a good move and one that has helped in dealing with legislation during this session in a more orderly fashion.
When I spoke on this subject at the time it came before the house last session I recall saying that in the planning of the business of a session the government itself had a good deal to do with the length of the session, and that good management and a program well arranged would invariably lead to a shortening of the session whereas ineffective management of the legislative program by those in charge would lead to delay. I pointed out that all the government needed to do to delay the proceedings of the house was to bring four or five controversial measures before parliament and then deal with each only one day at a time in a kind of round

robin process, and that under such a procedure the session could last indefinitely. However, when the government brings forward a measure, initiates a debate and allows the debate to continue until the subject has been dealt with, I think the government then contributes to an orderly expedition of the business of the session.
The change in the rules as to time, referred to by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition applies to members other than these two hon. gentlemen. Unlimited time, of course, is also the right of a person moving a government measure and of the first speaker from the opposition replying to a government motion. I think some progress could be made in setting a time limit in this regard. I would not say that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition should agree never to speak longer than one hour. The Prime Minister may feel that would	increase	the	effectiveness	of	thespeeches of the Leader of the Opposition, or the Leader of the Opposition might think it would	increase	the	effectiveness	of	the
speeches of the Prime Minister. However, when it comes to people who are replying for the opposition I believe there might be a limit of one hour, shall we say, or perhaps a limit of 40 minutes might be applied, without reducing the rights and without reducing the effectiveness of the opposition.
There has been a feeling in some quarters from time to time that we might remove the committee stage preceding money bills. This is a proposal with which I would be unable to agree. I feel that is a very valuable stage of any debate. I think it is a stage, wisely used and seriously considered by the government, which could lead to important changes in the legislation that would follow. I feel this stage enables the members, in a free sense, to deal with the particular principles of the question under discussion.
I would think the committee, Mr. Speaker, should give some serious consideration to the procedures of the committees of this house. I do not believe the committees of this house perform as useful a service as they might, since they seem so often to be the captives of the government majority. I believe individual members should have the right to call for persons and papers and should have a good deal to do with the agenda of the committee. Consideration should be given also to the reports that are made by committees. I do not like to see the practice being followed which seems to have grown up, not under this administration only but under previous administrations as well, namely that a committee of this house that is dealing with a piece of controversial legislation will make a recommendation and, since it is a hot

Appointment of Committee on House Rules
potato, since the government does not want to deal with it, the recommendation is brought to the house but concurrence in the report of the committee is not moved.
I think if a committee brings a report to the house, then the house should have an opportunity to debate the recommendations contained therein. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, the country can be very easily misled into thinking that far greater weight has been given to the recommendations of the committee than is in fact the case. I would refer to a particular instance that I have in mind, namely the report of the agriculture committee dealing with the feed grain and feed mill situation. On June 27 the committee made certain recommendations which were reported to the house. However, the report was never moved in the house. The country has been led to believe that the report of this committee had a very wide measure of approval. The fact of the matter is that it was such a hot, controversial issue, I suggest, and the government felt so uncertain, that no step was taken by any member of the party opposite to move this report of the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but he is going rather far afield. It seems to me he is threshing old straw in dealing with the merits of the report of the agriculture committee at this time.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
I was not dealing with the merits. I was just dealing with the fact that it was a controversial issue and, being a controversial issue, when a report was made to the house no one on the opposite side of the house cared to move the report. I think this makes something of a farce of the so-called recommendations coming from the committee, and it certainly leaves a situation that could be misinterpreted in the country. I suggest that in order to give greater weight to the recommendations of committees, the procedure committee should consider whether or not, when particular recommendations are made, the report should be considered and either approved or rejected by the house itself.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this committee on procedure made another reference of great interest and great importance but not quite so precise as certain other recommendations. It is found at the bottom of page 827 of Votes and Proceedings for July 25, 1960, and reads as follows:
In addition, the committee has given preliminary consideration to a number of other procedural problems and has initiated studies which will assist in a more comprehensive review of the matters referred to it.
It is therefore recommended that a similar committee be appointed early in the next session to
carry on these studies including the procedure on private bills of divorce which the committee has been asked and is willing to consider in so far as the problem is capable of procedural solution.
We are in a very difficult position, Mr. Speaker, with respect to this question at this moment, in that we are not certain whether the members of another place are going to approve a bill that was approved by this house. Parliament itself, therefore, may have given its stamp of approval to a procedure for the handling of private bills of divorce different from the cumbersome, awkward and exasperating system that has been in vogue for many years. The constitutionality of this procedure has been raised. I am not a constitutional authority. Since I am a farmer, perhaps my attitude on this question is just too simple. My attitude is that if a thing works, let us approve it. Of course I know the constitutional authorities will look at the matter exceedingly carefully to see if parliament has gone beyond its right in dealing with the matter, and I agree that such a look is important.
If it should, and I hope this is not the case, be necessary for the committee to deal with this question in the light of the old procedure, I hope it will be able to make some recommendations that will result in removing consideration of divorce bills from this House of Commons, while granting to the people who are involved the rights and protection that come from established legal procedures.
The Leader of the Opposition said he did not wish to speak too long. He was in favour of the motion, and he wanted action on this subject. Well, there is good reason to pass this motion on its own merits. There are other good reasons, namely the statistics on the continuing unemployment situation, which suggest to all members of parliament in January, as they did in November, that the House of Commons, parliament and the government have not yet effectively dealt with this situation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past two sessions of parliament I have had the privilege of serving on the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Indian affairs which was established by a resolution, as intimated by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in April, 1959. This committee continued to operate during last session and heard a great number of submissions and briefs from nearly every Indian tribe and reservation, supported by various competent speakers.
The sum total of all these meetings was "the conclusion drawn by several members that our Indians were more than justified in asking for a revision of the act which would give them the same rights as those enjoyed by all Canadians.
The mere change or amendment of the act will not bring immediate integration of the Indian population. Before we can obtain Ihe desired result it will require patience, guidance and financial assistance by both federal and provincial governments. The ultimate objective, however, should be a full integration of Indians and whites, which can be seen bearing fruit in several parts of [DOT]Canada.
As an example I will refer you to what has taken place in the Kenora district of northwestern Ontario. There a public school which had 75 pupils accepted 50 Indian students, and it was found that there is no intellectual difference between them and the white pupils. The principal of that school made an observation to the effect that while a slow Indian student may be slightly slower than a slow white student, a bright Indian child is every bit the equal of a bright white child. The principal of this school-and I wish that we had more principals like him -made the statement that the younger Indian children integrated with the white children immediately, and that the older ones took longer only because they were shy. However, he is certain that if this policy of integration continues, even the slightest variations of racial behaviour will in time disappear.
A special effort should be made to ensure that no Indian pupil will be deprived of the benefit of secondary education. A definite policy should be established by the Indian affairs branch, in co-operation with the provincial departments of education and school boards, in order to make sure that every Indian boy and girl be encouraged to attend high school, vocational and technical school. Where necessary assistance should be provided for transportation and in some cases also for noon meals during the school period. I also strongly urge the government to set
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act up scholarships to be given to pupils qualifying for higher education. This is a most important feature and it should receive the hearty approval of the minister, who has shown a sympathetic understanding of the serious need to improve the educational standard of our first citizens.
I am told that while the doors of immigration are partially closed to most classifications of trades and labour they are wide open for trained domestics. I offer no criticism of this. I do, however, suggest that we are passing up an excellent opportunity by not making an effort to make use of a great number of girls living on reserves. Why not set up special classes in our elementary or vocational schools? Why not institute a training program for young Indian girls to train them in household duties, child care and a general idea of what to expect in domestic service? This would be assistance of inestimable value.
While the Indian on the reserve retains many of the traditions of his forefathers, some of the traditions have been dropped. The heredity principle, if not altogether scrapped, has been greatly modified as can be seen through the present method of choosing chiefs. Chiefs are now elected in very much the same way as our own communities elect their mayors. These elections are the cornerstones of a new era of democracy on the reserves which might well pave the way to self-determination among the first Canadians.
Last year Indian chiefs and counsellors from reserves scattered throughout northwestern Ontario met at a conference in the Quetico training centre. They went through a course of training under the direction of officials from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Indian affairs branch, and I am sure the minister has a full report of this meeting. This course was designed to bring better understanding of the responsibility of leadership that rests with the chiefs and counsellors in the reserve.

speechtext:
I will modify my remarks to conform with your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I would say that the Canadian Indian, to whom I shall refer during my remarks as the first Canadian, by virtue of legislation passed at the last session, is now a full-fledged voting citizen with representation in the Senate, and here I should like to record the facts that in 1940 a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons recommended to the government of the day that the federal franchise be extended to all Indians. Unfortunately opposition developed among some of the Indians themselves, as a result of which the parliament of that day decided not to put the committee recommendation into effect. As indicated by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) it appears there is still some opposition today to this worth-while recommendation, but I point out that these objections will in time wear out. It has taken 20 years for opposition to the voting privilege to wear down to the point where this privilege is being accepted as a right.
May I say for the information of the house that on September 26, 1959, at my invitation, Senator James Gladstone visited the reserve at Fort William. The city council tendered a luncheon in his honour, and in the evening a large meeting of several hundred Indians and others was held at Chippewa park. The reception was held under the auspices of the board of parks management who supplied the refreshments.
Chief Frank Pelletier of Fort William acted as chairman and arranged a pow-wow to celebrate the visit. All in all, it was a great day for these people.
I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to express the grateful thanks of my constituents to the senator who represents all the


Indians of Canada for his keen interest in their welfare, an interest which he has demonstrated by making personal contacts and visiting Indian communities across the country.
Notwithstanding the recognition that Indians should enjoy equal rights with all. Canadians the truth of the matter is that they do not by any means possess those equal, rights. Take, for example, the case of an Indian ex-serviceman in my own constituency, who on the field of battle won no less than six medals. Yet this man was denied the-privilege of having a bottle of beer in his home. His name is David Kimball of the Fort William Indian reserve. He was charged for having beer in his home. He was fined $70 and costs, or 50 days in jail. When he appeared before the magistrate-and I quote his remarks as reported in the press-he said: "I fought for this country. They gave me six medals. They advertise beer on T.V., but I can't bring it home. I plead guilty." The magistrate told him that he had to obey the law as it was presently constituted, and that until a change was made Indians could not have alcohol on the reserve.
Of course, this is no indictment of the magistrate. It is the law which should be changed. Here I should like to point out that there is a clear responsibility on the part of the Indian affairs branch to inaugurate an adult education program by means of films, lectures and reading material to make the Indians realize the dangers of alcoholism and its effect on their homes and social life.
Unless substantial changes are made in the Indian Act, changes or amendments which will give these people opportunities and privileges equal to those enjoyed by all citizens, the bill of rights which was so ceremoniously introduced during the last session of parliament will remain only a limited declaration of intentions.
The question of rights and privileges for Indians is so confused that there is little wonder that so many petitions and briefs were presented to the committee during the last two sessions of parliament. The bill of rights in its present form does not protect the Indians. To be effective it requires that a number of changes be made in the Indian Act. I dare say that a considerable number of Indian leaders are demanding that necessary changes be made in order that whatever privileges may exist under the bill of rights be extended to them. One of them has to do-with the title of reserve lands and the right of Indians to own lands, the lands comprising' the reserves used by their ancestors for centuries and the homes which have been built on them.

Owning property is one of the principal rights which is recognized in the bill of rights as one of the freedoms but as the title to the reserves is in the name of the crown the Indians are barred from owning their own land. Therefore, under the present act, the Indian can obtain a certificate indicating possession but he cannot sell or transfer the title to anyone not a member of the band, the whole purpose being to prevent a break-up of the reservation. That is the reason why some groups made representations to the committee urging the abolition of the certificate system in order that all lands be held in one parcel.
The restriction imposed on the sale of land only to another member of the band will militate against his being able to obtain a fair price for his property, a practice which of course is not in keeping with the fundamental freedoms enunciated in the bill of rights.
Another flagrant violation of human rights is suffered by an Indian girl if she happens to marry a non-Indian. In that event under the provisions of the present Indian Act she ceases to be an Indian and is disqualified to inherit her father's property or home.
Mr. Stewart Udall, a member of the United States house of representatives, who was recently appointed secretary of the interior by president-elect John F. Kennedy, immediately after his appointment made this statement:
We have not done enough for our Indian citizens -we can do and intend to do a better job.
That is precisely the spirit in which this resolution should be accepted by all members of the house irrespective of where we sit. No lesser objective and determination should be shown by the government in dealing with amendments to the present Indian Act which should be expected to be brought into this house at the earliest possible moment.
The department should consider the establishment of modern fish processing plants which would encourage many Indians to enter into the commercial fishing field. As an example, Armstrong Fisheries was organized by a group of commercial fishermen in northwestern Ontario which will operate a processing plant at Pickle lake, capable of handling one million pounds of fish a year. This plant will provide good cash returns to the Indian population of the district of Patricia.

I now pass on the subject of education which I feel is paramount. Indeed, in my opinion it is the key to a successful contribution toward a higher standard of living for our first citizens who have for far too long suffered economic inequalities in relation to the white man, inequalities in opportunities for education, inequalities in opportunities for employment in various occupations, inequalities in cases of public welfare apart from the treaty pittance which is doled out annually on the reserves. What is needed, in short, is a recognition of the right of the Indians to equality with all Canadians.
These people feel, and not without some justification, that they have been neglected. They point out the difference between the white communities and the slums on their reserves. They feel deprived of the opportunity to make a reasonable living on the reserve and sometimes despair as to what should be done about it.
In the brief presented by the Blackfoot Indians to the joint parliamentary committee during the last session they suggested changes which called for a reform of the entire structure of Indian policy and a program of assistance. I wish to quote from an article written by William Morris which appeared in the magazine section of the Globe and Mail of December 3, 1960:
Answers will not be found until the government takes a new look at its entire treatment of the Canadian Indian. Radical changes will have to be made in its legislative program and the administration of the Indian affairs branch-both long overdue. At a recent meeting of the joint parliamentary committee on Indian affairs, the Black-foot Indians pressed for such a sweeping change. But they believe that the government, which while in opposition appeared to be their champion, is not capable of giving them the leadership they badly need.
They have good reason for their belief. In its 3 j years of power, the government of John Diefenbaker has failed to introduce any policy which would come to grips with a major question affecting Indians.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall forgo the reading of the rest of the quotation, which, in my view, is important in relation to the question we are discussing, namely the purpose of the establishment of the committee. In my view its purpose is to


rectify any injustices which have been perpetrated upon the Indian people up to now. That is the only purpose. In any event I shall forgo the reading of this particular article which is very good indeed. I commend it to every member of the committee.
It has been established, of course, that more and more of our first Canadians are becoming integrated into city life and are leaving the reserves. Some have made a success as farmers, tourist camp and gas filling station operators, and in dozens of other trades and professions. Therefore, there is no valid reason to believe that they cannot succeed in fields which up to now have been considered as the white man's preserves. All they need is education and training.
In answer to one of my questions, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) assured the house that the vocational training provided under Bill No. C-49 would apply to Indians on the reserves. I express the hope that the Indians on the Fort William reserve, as on all the reserves in Canada, will avail themselves of this opportunity, because it is the kind of assistance that I have been advocating ever since my election to parliament.
I also wish to point out to the minister that the method by which men are selected for training under this scheme should be such that it will not discriminate against applicants from the reserves, and that adequate assistance be given to them while they are in training to the same extent as it is given to others. The minister said that the selection would be the responsibility of the provinces. While I do not think that the provincial authorities will discriminate in any way against Indians, nevertheless I should like to suggest that a special recommendation on behalf of the Indians be made by the minister to those who will have charge of approving the applicants for vocational training as outlined in the legislation.
The Glenbow foundation, which is a charitable institution organized in Calgary, has recently submitted a recommendation urging the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to give consideration to the enactment of legislation to protect archaeological remains or sites on Indian reserves, especially in areas which are threatened with destruction by excavation for power projects and other developments. I commend this suggestion to the minister as being worthy of serious consideration, with the added recommendation that in this work of preservation of historical sites preference for employment be given to local Indians.

I cannot think of anything more appropriate to conclude my remarks on this important and challenging subject than to quote a few sentences from a report of the Indian-Eskimo association of Canada:
We see that there has to be a continuing effort to create among the Indians, material well-being, civic sense, and social cohesions. We do not see how present safeguarding of the peculiar Indian rights and present enforcement of their disabilities can be combined harmoniously with their journeying to the good life.
I submit that while there may not be easy solutions of the various questions which I have endeavoured to bring to the attention of this house, I do believe however that if we approach the problem with good will and determination, satisfactory results will be produced to the end that our first Canadians will eventually share with all other Canadians the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few comments on the motion before us I too, like the hon. member who has just resumed his seat and also the minister, of course, look with great expectations upon the establishment of this committee and the results which we hope will flow from it.
As the minister indicated, the committee last session made a unanimous recommendation with respect to the compulsory enfranchisement section of the act, recommending that it be removed. I do not think there is anyone in the country who would disagree with that recommendation. Had the government moved with alacrity and undertaken to accept the bill that I introduced last session and again this session they could have accomplished that object, namely the deletion of section 112 from the Indian Act. This course is still open to the minister. In fact, it would mean less work for her if the government adopted the bill I now have on the order paper for the elimination of section 112, and that could be done without any difficulty.
During last session and the session before it was my privilege to be a member of the committee and I hope I shall have the opportunity to be a member during this session. There are, of course, others of my colleagues in the C.C.F. party who have an intense interest in Indian affairs. Owing to our democratic process of electing members to the committee I may have some difficulty in overcoming their desires but I hope I shall be successful.
I for one expect that the committee will have sufficient opportunity and length of time at its disposal not only to conclude its hearings during the present session but also
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act to conclude its work with respect to all details, the most important of which, of course, is the making of recommendations to parliament for amendments to the act and changes in administration and other Indian affairs.
I think these recommendations must be couched in the most definite terms. I do not think they should be to any degree wishy-washy or hopeful that certain circumstances will develop. As I have said, they should be strong and definite and as all-inclusive as possible, covering all facets of the problems confronting our native Indian people. There should, of course, be a striving toward unanimity of the committee with respect to whatever recommendations it produces. In my opinion, the stronger, the more definite and conclusive these recommendations are, the better the chance will be of their becoming a reality in statute form and in policy and administrative procedures on the part of the government in office.
Our attitude in the past toward our native Indian people is something of which we should not be too proud. I have mentioned a number of times in the house and elsewhere that the history of our treatment of our native Indian people leaves a great deal to be desired. We-when I say "we" I mean the non-Indian population because in this relationship I do not think the term "white man" is correct-in effect have ruined their economic structure without attempting to replace it with something else with which they can cope. To a great extent we have disregarded their historical background, their arts and their culture without bending too much effort even to understand or appreciate them and have attempted to force them to accept our way of life.
We have discriminated against them in employment, in educational opportunities and in other ways too. To a great extent we have disregarded their rights as individuals and as a group of people. A recent case in point is the action of the government of British Columbia in its almost callous invasion of the Kitwanga reserve in my constituency for the purpose of building a highway. When I say "callous invasion" that is just what I mean. Officials invaded the reserve without even the initial courtesy of writing a letter to anybody saying that this was going to be done, and subsequently they were forced to sit down and negotiate with respect to the value of the land taken and the timber destroyed. That is just one recent example of attitudes that have been displayed in the past.
I hope that this committee after its extensive hearings and consideration of the matters before it will be able to make a start on reversing past actions and attitudes so that our native Indian population can have all the
1178	HOUSE OF
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act opportunities available to other citizens of this nation, so that they can develop their individual potentials, so that they can live a fuller life, so that their culture and history can be absorbed by us to help to enrich our culture and history.
One of the most important things leading toward this end which should be considered by the committee and by everyone concerned is the question of education. I refer not only to the type of formal education we have in mind when we think of children going to school but also to adult education because a great many elderly native Indian people are still illiterate so far as our language is concerned, never having had the opportunity to attend school. They have never had a chance to absorb our ideas or to impart to us their own ideas. Education should be extended to include adults also but with more importance being placed on the children because the native Indian children of our nation in the same way as other children are the ones who hold the future of their race and of our society in their hands. They are the ones who will be making the greatest strides toward assimilation, integration or whatever term you wish to use in dealing with the relationship between Indian people and nonIndian people.
I think the committee should consider that education should not be confined solely to the teaching of traditional school subjects such as reading, writing, arithmetic, etc. I envisage an amalgamated school system and, hoping that the committee may consider it favourably also, I hope that the committee will take into account teaching native Indian people about their way of life in the past, their history and their background and also teaching our children the same thing so that all of us can benefit by the process of education.
I think the committee should look carefully into the experience gained in past years through the use of the so-called amalgamated schools. Under this system the Indian affairs branch enters into an agreement with a local school board for the teaching of Indian children in schools under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. The Indian affairs branch pays a certain per capita amount and in some cases contributes toward the capital cost of construction of schools or additions thereto. This is an important thing. It is a new development in the last 10 or 12 years and to quite an etxent it is still considered by some to be an experiment.
This matter should be carefully considered by the committee, for it is my hope that the eventual result will be that all our native Indian children will be taught in schools


under provincial jurisdiction where non-Indian children are taught. As quickly as possible and as much as possible the Indian affairs branch should get out of the picture so far as education is concerned so that it will all be under provincial jurisdiction.
The basis for this argument, of course, is a simple one, equality of treatment. This is one thing which I think the members of the committee should always keep in their minds, that we should look toward the placing of our native Indian children in such schools on an equal basis and there should be equal rights and responsibilities resting upon all of us in this regard.
There is another question of general importance but of more importance in some parts of the nation than others and of more importance to some individual native Indians than others. I refer to the question of liquor rights. As I say, some people have more interest in this than others.

speechtext:
On the point of order you have raised, Mr. Speaker, there is what one would call divided jurisdiction in this field. The Indian Act deals with the question of liquor as it relates to Indians and provincial statutes also apply in this field. A most discriminatory situation results from this twofold jurisdiction. The Indian Act provides that they cannot have liquor and then it says that they can have liquor under certain circumstances and in certain parts of the province, depending on what the province says. This is discriminatory. In so far as liquor is concerned, in British Columbia we treat our native Indian people not even as second class citizens but perhaps as third or fourth class citizens, more as children than as adults.
We have had a Social Credit government in that province for some eight years. They have continued this discrimination by refusing to act. In fact, I would say they have done nothing in the field of Indian affairs in all the years they have been in office. However, this is a provincial matter. There are references in the Indian Act itself, which this committee will be considering, to liquor and its relationship to the native Indian people. The committee might very well consider, therefore, the question of removing the federal government entirely from jurisdiction in so far as liquor is concerned, removing all the sections in the Indian Act that relate to liquor. The basis for this argument is equality of

treatment, equality of rights and responsibility. The provincial governments might be left to legislate in the field of liquor as they see fit. I believe this procedure would remove one of the most unfair parts of the statute as it relates to this particular social matter. The basic point from which to start is consideration of equality of rights, equality of responsibility. If the other citizens of this nation desire to have a drink of liquor of some sort, they do not have to resort to a bootlegger and pay $10, $15 or even $25 for a bottle of cheap, rotgut whisky. The only reason the Indians have to do this is the fact that they are Indians.
I was just reading a newspaper article which recites some of the results from this state of affairs. The Vancouver Sun of January 17-

I do not wish to contravene your ruling in any way, Mr. Speaker. I was simply going to make reference to an occurrence that would point up the necessity of the committee giving this matter intense consideration because the lives of people are involved. The Vancouver Sun of yesterday points out that 14 people became seriously ill on a reserve at Kamloops, one of them is still blinded and two others died as a result of a drinking party. They made the error of drinking methyl hydrate, which is rather poisonous. This occurrence just illustrates the results of these unfair and discriminatory liquor laws. I think the committee should take this into account because it is more than just a social problem when people's lives are involved.
The committee should give intense consideration to the field of health and welfare, A number of submissions have been made to the committee on these subjects in past sessions. In this field again we are, in effect, saying there is twofold jurisdiction because in so far as the Indian people are concerned the federal parliament can legislate and in so far as the various provinces are concerned they, too, can legislate with regard to matters of health and welfare which affect the residents of those provinces. It would seem to me the committee should give adequate consideration to whether the federal government should take the step of transferring jurisdiction over Indians in the field of health and 90205-6-75
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act welfare to the provincial governments who now have extensive health and welfare departments established. Perhaps this step would eliminate such cases as the 90 school children who received some public attention recently when they had to have teeth extracted. This caused some furore and resentment amongst the Indian people against the department of health and welfare, the Indian affairs branch and everybody else.
The committee should consider another matter of extreme importance, namely the economic development and the economic opportunities available to native Indian people, especially on our reserves. Their employment opportunities are restricted now even more than by the collapse of our economy generally occasioned by this government. Their employment opportunities are restricted primarily because of the fact they are native Indians and have not had the educational background necessary to enable them to fit in to our type of economy, even when it was running properly. This is a matter to which the committee, I believe, should give intense consideration.
I believe the Indian affairs branch itself realizes this is a problem, and has realized it for some time. In fact, the annual report of the department for the year ending March 31, 1960 refers to the problem of employment opportunities and the economic difficulties that native Indian people encounter when they try to compete in the various areas outside of their reserves. Many of these people, because of a lack of education or because they were channelled into particular types of employment, now find their economic life rests on one form of employment and they have not the ability to move to another type of employment. I know that on the coast of British Columbia, for instance, almost the entire economic life of the native Indian population rests upon the fishing industry. Their chances of expanding into other fields of employment are rather restricted. This is something the committee must take into consideration and I think must correlate with its consideration of the educational question.
Another matter to which the committee should give some attention is one which is often referred to in my province as the B.C. land question. Unless a solution is found to this particular land question the chance of advancing very far in other fields is somewhat limited. I know the Indians of British Columbia, for instance, claim that, apart from a couple of small sections, they have never extinguished or relinquished their title to the land in that province. There are no treaties in British Columbia except those connected with the one or two small areas to which I referred. The Indians say, in fact, that the
1180	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act land upon which the provincial legislature building is situated is properly owned by them. This is a problem that has rankled them for many years and to which they have tried to find a solution. I feel the committee could help to find that solution by recommending negotiations by the government for the purchase of the land. Perhaps a court decision will be necessary to determine whether the Indians in fact have title to the land. I think they do.
The government, as we know, has already established a policy of re-negotiating treaties with the Indians. If they are willing to renegotiate certain treaties then we can assume the government would negotiate a treaty where none now exists. This is a question of property rights and equality of treatment of the people. If I own land or if you own land, Mr. Speaker, you have title to it and you have the opportunity of relinquishing that title. Unless a solution is found to this most important problem in British Columbia it will continue to remain a barrier between the native Indian people and the non-Indian people in these other fields I have mentioned such as education, housing, welfare and liquor rights.
I think my remarks should be drawn to a close now. As I said, Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely wide, broad and important field, and one in which I myself have an intense interest. I have a deep desire to see justice obtained for these people. This committee can start a reversal of the process that has taken place in the last 100 years or so in Canada. They can start us back on the road toward equality of treatment for our native Indian people. They can start us back on the road to the extension of justice to these people in all of their problems. They can start us back on the road of making provision for them to have an honourable existence; a full, secure and peaceful life; and equal opportunities for themselves and for their children in the same way as they are available to others of us in this nation.
The native Indian people I know, and with whom I have communicated and have spoken, are looking toward this committee with great expectations. Many of them have written letters to the committee itself. Many have appeared and presented briefs. Some of them were short, others were extensive and well documented. They are looking to this committee for a solution to their many problems. The committee has a great responsibility resting upon its shoulders with regard to the treatment of our native Indian peoples in Canada. I certainly hope that this committee does not disappoint these native people.

-and to suggest such amendments as they may deem advisable, with authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, on the social and economic status of the Indians.

My only suggestion at this time stems from a conversation I had during the Christmas recess with one of the chaplains on an Indian reserve in my own riding. I refer to the Big Cove reservation. These are the two suggestions that were expressed to me by this chaplain and I should like to impart them to the minister at this time.

I perhaps should say that this reservation is now possessed of adequate school facilities but that one of the handicaps is that no vocational training is being given in these schools. It would seem that vocational training is essential if we wish to improve the economic status of the people living upon this reservation. The suggestion advanced by this chaplain was this. Of course I should perhaps say that all the people living on this reservation are of the same faith. Before the minister replies, Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a matter that has been brought to my attention by some of those who are dealing with the Indians in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. It is true that I should like to be on the Indian affairs committee but I do not represent any Indians of a reservation nature. There are no reservations in my riding. However, I have some interest in the problems in the adjoining areas that have reservations.
In talking to a gentleman who has an influence on and is closely connected with a number of mission schools in the Hudson bay area I was interested in some of the comments he was making. A year or two ago I had discussed the problem of enfranchising the Indians, some of the problems that might be expected to result from that franchise, and the fears that the Indians themselves were expressing. I was pleased to hear from him the other day that these fears had in the main been allayed.
He was telling me that they have a problem that the Indian affairs officials in the mission are in no way able to deal with, namely the problem of taking the children of Indians, particularly of those who go into the bush in the winter, and asking them to reside in schools with other Indian families or in boarding schools for short periods of time. He pointed out to me that seldom do the children ever get more than four years in school on this basis. It has been the practice in the last two or three years to get children in these schools from the age of 12 years to 16 years. They are beyond the normal school age when they get them. They have been with their families who travel into the bush in the winter time. When the family goes out in the fall they may be persuaded to leave one or two of these children with the mission or with one of the schools.
Those members of the family who do go into the bush learn in an Indian way the
90205-6-'75J
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act abilities of their forefathers. They learn in the bush itself to pursue the family tradition and to successfully follow the pursuits in which the family has been engaged for generations. The children who attend school, and who may receive four years of formal education, do so at a time when they would normally be learning to carry on in the footsteps of their forefathers. By the time they are 16 they are satisfied with schooling but are no longer able to return to the particular occupations available to Indians who have not had the opportunity of attending schools. Thus it means they have been deprived of part of their normal education, an education which they would have received if they had followed their families.

Broadcasting
recognize there is a great deal left to be done. Possibly I could transgress the rules long enough to say that today 90 per cent of all Indians of school age attend school. This, I think, is a great improvement. Moreover, the situation continues to improve almost from day to day.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) was insistent on scholarships. We already have scholarships. In fact, there are 44 scholarships of various types available for which Indian children can compete, and I say, further, that any Indian student who demonstrates a capacity to absorb knowledge can acquire just as much education as he is able to absorb. This is the result of a progressive policy which has grown over the years. The whole problem of education will only be solved in a matter of time as these people become more and more convinced of the necessity of encouraging their children to acquire as much education as they possibly can.
Once more, I do not want to try to answer all the various pleas that have been made, because you, Mr. Speaker, have already told us that this type of debate is out of order, and I think it is. However, I did not want to let all the comments which have been made on this educational question remain on the record without throwing some light on the situation as it is at the present time.
I should like to thank hon. members for their participation in this discussion, and I trust that when the committee meets they will throw their efforts wholeheartedly into the work of this committee and give us and the Indians every assistance in the direction of clarifying the requirements of the Indians today in an effort to produce for them an act more in keeping with the present day circumstances.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that Your Honour has drawn attention to the vagueness of the motion and that it has been underlined by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) because I think it will be very difficult for the minister, the Chair or anyone else to rule out of order anything that I may choose to say about this motion so long as it has any vague reference to broadcasting.
I have complained, sir, and I complain again at the outset, about this motion. We in the opposition do not want a vague and general reference. We have asked over and over again for a specific and particular reference to which

we feel we have been entitled as a result of an understanding which we believed was reached with the government at the time the present Broadcasting Act was enacted in 1958.
At that time we forewent the right to have this bill sent to a special committee at the request of the government in order to enable the bill to get through in that session in a reasonable time. We understood that when a committee was set up the first task entrusted to that committee-and that the terms of reference of the committee would so indicate -would be to examine the operation of the Broadcasting Act clause by clause so that we could see how it was really operating, because we in the opposition took as strong exception to certain sections of that act at that time as we have taken to any legislation which has been introduced in this house by the present government and we believe the experience with that act has shown that the exceptions we took to that legislation were soundly based.
We realize that because of our conventions in this house the opposition will be in a minority in the committee as it is in the house. I am not complaining about that fact. We also realize that unless the terms of reference are specific it will be possible for the majority, as has happened previously when committees on this subject have been set up, to introduce other matters and vote down our efforts to carry out what we believed was the inquiry pledged to us by the government.
I hope that before this motion is passed the minister will see fit to have one of his colleagues propose an amendment to indicate that in the investigation to be conducted by the committee priority should be given to a clause by clause examination of the act. Otherwise, the opposition-of this I feel quite confident-will once again be denied the opportunity to carry out that investigation because the majority of that committee, which was not very respectful of the minister two years ago as the hon. gentleman will recall, will pay no attention and will proceed to ride their own horses.
I am not complaining about that, either. If the motion is left vague and indefinite they have, of course, every right to do that. The undertaking which we understood was given to us by the government should, I feel, be carried out in good faith by the government and I am once more asking that this be done.
Unlike the Minister of National Revenue, I am not a lawyer and I have ceased even the formal study of law. In order to remove some misapprehension in the house I thought this a suitable occasion to make a public declaration to that effect. On a careful appraisal
Broadcasting
of the matter I have come to the conclusion that there are other fields of endeavour which perhaps may be more immediately rewarding and in which, perhaps, the fictions do not necessarily need to be legal. However, I am afraid I am, even on the vague terms of this resolution, somewhat out of order at this moment and so I come back to the resolution itself.
As I say, if I read this language correctly, there is no matter herein referred to that is going to be before this committee on a strict reading of this motion unless "radio and television broadcasting" can be described as matters, and "broadcasting" is a singular noun and therefore it seems to me it would be hard for it to be "matters". It does not seem, therefore, that the motion in its present form makes any sense at all. I intend to suggest that there should be certain priorities given and the highest priority, I repeat again, should be the carrying out of what we understood to be the undertaking given by the government in 1958.
The second matter that I believe the committee ought to discuss is that of the granting of private television licences in those communities where the C.B.C. has up till now had the exclusive licence. This has been a matter of great public controversy particularly in the city of Toronto where notwithstanding the fact that the board of broadcast governors said they had the greatest difficulty discriminating between the nine applicants, they chose to give the licence to one of those which was also a newspaper. I would not have cared which newspaper it was, I would have objected, because I think that when the applicants are equally good a licence should not be given to the proprietors of a newspaper. If they are not equally good, that is another matter, and there are some places where that is the case. I must say, speaking for my personal preference, that the newspaper chosen would be the last newspaper to which I would have granted a licence in Toronto, or practically anywhere else, but that is a matter of bias, sir.

speechtext: The Toronto Star would be slightly ahead of it, I suppose?

speechtext:
Or even the Globe and Mail, Mr. Speaker, even the Globe and Mail. I just do not happen to like the Toronto Telegram and I have the impression that they reciprocate my feeling, but that again is a little beyond the vague terms of this motion.
As I say, the second matter for discussion should be the principles on which these exclusive licences-because that is what they are, licences of bits of the public domain; that is what the privy council said this was

Broadcasting
-are given to one person rather than another person, and I use the word "person" in the legal sense. This is a matter of the greatest possible moment and one about which I think parliament properly should be concerned.
The third matter to which I feel the committee should direct its attention is the problem of the financing of the C.B.C. My views on this subject and the views of my friends in the house are well known. We take the position that the Fowler commission and all preceding royal commissions on this matter were right when they said that the financing of public broadcasting should not be dependent upon the whim of the government or based upon annual votes by parliament for the reason I have stated many times before in this house but which cannot be stated too often, that the moment an agency has to come to the treasury board and argue its case it becomes a creature not of parliament but of the government no matter how many safeguards of theoretical independence are put into the legislation.
In those circumstances human nature being what it is there will be an inevitable tendency-it may be repressed by persons of very high character but it should not be necessary to have it repressed-to lick the boots of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and of other members of the government in the hope of getting a little more largesse.
My view is that public broadcasting, like the courts, should be guaranteed its income by parliament in such a fashion that there is no incentive whatsoever to this kind of action. As the Fowler commission said, there should be some formula-and there are many formulae that might be used-for a period of years, at least sufficient to be slightly longer than the life of any one parliament, during which the revenues are fixed.

speechtext: The subject which the hon. member is now debating is really not the issue of the motion, and if he pursues it, of course, then other members will be entitled to debate the whole issue of how the C.B.C. should be financed. I take the view, rightly or wrongly, that the motion is to set up the committee and is not a review of the whole of the matters to be referred to the committee. It is simply a request to the house, and it is for the house to decide whether a committee is or is not desirable at this time, and that is a relatively narrow field of debate.

I must say that with a restraint which I do not often exercise, I listened in silence to rulings this afternoon which I must say startled me very much.

sir, if I may say so with the greatest possible respect, because I have been observing the proceedings of this house since the year 1937, and I have seen debates on the setting up of committees go on for days and days, and I have never before heard it suggested that all we should consider is whether or not is is expedient to have a committee at all.
I know that one can go back into the rules, particularly the rules at Westminster, as was the case, of course, in another similar matter in another debate to which I cannot refer as a precedent. But a wholly different practice, I think, has been consecrated in this house, perhaps wrongly. It may be one of those wrongs that is consecrated, surely, by so much modern usage and by so many accretions of custom that I think it would be quite restrictive of what are deemed, and what have come to be regarded as the rights of parliament, to suggest that the matters which are going to come before the committee should not have, I do not say extended debate, but some consideration on such motions.
And I might add, sir, in this particular case there seems to be the additional circumstance that there is no specification of what the matters are that are to come before this committee, and I am appealing to the minister to put a list of those matters in. I was seeking to justify the importance of putting this particular question in and also seeking to establish certain priorities in the order of these matters. However, I think I have sufficiently made my point with respect to this matter of financing. To me, the financing-

rule. I know the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate can give sanctions of usage which have gone a long way to deprecate the importance of the rule. speechtext: I would agree with that. I take the opportunity of rising again because I think this is a matter of some consequence. It does arise from time to time. I do not want to be running counter to the wishes of the house or to be unduly restrictive. The point of view I took would permit reference to the various matters. It seems to me to be unreasonable for the house to spell out in detail all the issues which are to be referred to the committee for the purpose of saving the time of the house. subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
If I may say so with deference, I cannot agree with the last view because we cannot deal with witnesses here and that is one of the most important functions of a committee. But I would not like to see the sense of the house taken without more debate and discussion. This is a very important point. If I may advert to something which came up earlier this afternoon. We had a motion to set up a committee to consider with Your Honour the rules of the house, and I would suggest that this might very usefully be considered by that committee; but that, in the meantime, we should be jealous not merely of the rules that are in the rule book at Westminster, or even the ancient precedents of this house, but that we should respect some of the modern precedents as well.
I remember on one occasion, sir, if I may just add this reminiscence, one of the best debates that ever took place in the house
Broadcasting
in which Mr. Drew, then leader of the opposition, and the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who was then minister of transport, participated and in which the whole broadcasting policy of the government was debated, if my recollection is right, for nearly two days, on a motion similar to this, without any question of consent having arisen. I do not offer this as a menace, sir, or even as an incentive; I merely recall it.
As I was saying, I do believe that this whole problem of financing does need consideration for the reason I have given and also for another reason which I intend to give without elaborating. I think that the cost of broadcasting-I know you can work it out at so many cents per head per day and it does not sound very much-to the treasury is a matter which must give even the reckless Minister of Finance we have at present some concern from time to time. This is another reason why I think this committee should give the most careful consideration to this matter.
There is another matter to which I think very careful consideration should be given. I refer to the question of the commercial policy of the public broadcasting system. In that regard, one of the reasons why the Aird commission recommended public broadcasting in the first place, and why every committee of the house and every commission that has ever considered the matter has recommended its continuation, was for the maintenance of a Canadian identity. I may say that I fully subscribe to that view and I have, I think, in my private life and in my public life, always been a supporter of public broadcasting for that reason and for that reason only because I do recognize the dangers of public broadcasting as they were manifest in some parts of Europe 25 years ago when some of us were rather younger than we are now and as they still exist today in many totalitarian countries. This is potentially a very dangerous instrument in the hands of an unscrupulous government and it needs to be safeguarded in every possible way against control by the government, as opposed to control by parliament itself in which people are freely elected whether or not the people who elect them like the government.
I say, sir, that this commercial policy is something which I think should be considered very carefully for this reason. Every morning I turn on station CBO just before I get up because I want to find out what the temperature is and some other things of that sort and then listen to the news. One thing that has been dinned into my mind in the last few weeks is that the most important message CBO has for us every morning is

Broadcasting
that we should buy the Saturday Evening Post and McCall's magazines. I do not see how you could be more ridiculous than that.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext: That is at 7.30. At five minutes to eight you find out where you should have your shirts laundered.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Here is this public agency spending millions of public money to preserve our Canadian identity while this same agency, which is supposed to be doing that, is doing business with people, among all the thousands of potential advertisers, who are trying to sell magazines not produced in this country, this at a time when the government is trying to undo an error it made a year or two ago by setting up a commission under a very distinguished and loquacious journalist to inquire into means of keeping Canadian magazine and periodicals alive. It does seem to me that as a mere matter of good taste and good judgment the management of the C.B.C. has erred very sadly in this particular case.
I know, and nobody has said it oftener than I, that we in this parliament should not substitute ourselves for the management of the C.B.C. and I do not intend to do so. But I have also said, when on the treasury benches, and I say now that I see no reason why because we are members of parliament we should not feel free to criticize the C.B.C. I say that applies to those who sit on the treasury benches. I do not take the narrow view that was taken by the hon. member for Eglinton and one or two gentlemen when they sat on this side of the house that a minister must never speak to anybody connected with the management of the C.B.C. I think that is utter nonsense. I do not think being a minister deprives one of one's rights as a citizen.
For a minister to bring pressure to bear on them is one thing but a minister should be just as free as anyone else to express an opinion and to criticize and the C.B.C. should be so independent that the minister's freedom will not in any way influence them in any improper sense. That is the ideal and I admit it is a very difficult ideal to achieve. It is an ideal toward which all of us in this house should strive, and it seems to me that is a vital and important thing.
As I have said so often, it is almost more important in the modern world but certainly just as important today to preserve the independence of public broadcasting from pressure by the executive as it is to preserve the independence of the judiciary from pressure by the executive. They should be on the same basis. We should be sure that this pervasive influence, broadcasting, much more pervasive than the press though less

lasting, will not become an engine of potential tyranny, however brief and however transitory that might be. Therefore I think it is most important that at all these points where this potential danger arises we should, as a committee, try to put partisanship aside and consider this matter from the point of view of the preservation of our free institutions. Quite frankly, if we lived a thousand miles from any other country, if Canada were an island with 18 million people on it, I am not so sure, taking everything into account, that I would feel that public broadcasting was necessary at all.
I do think, considering the situation we have in Canada, that we have achieved a pretty good compromise between public and private broadcasting, but it is a compromise and the boundary line is and always will be,
I think, a somewhat fluctuating one. I do not think it can be a hard and fast line. In that context I think it is desirable that the committee should give consideration to the continuing place of private broadcasting in the whole national structure of broadcasting. In this context I should simply like to affirm again the view that, after three years' experience and notwithstanding the many criticisms I would make of the board of broadcast governors as at present constituted, I do think that the Fowler proposal that there should be a board of broadcast governors was a sound proposal that should be continued.
But, and here again this is another matter that I think the committee should consider, I think the committee should give very careful consideration, which of course would be done if my first suggestion that the act should be the first matter to be considered by the committee were carried out, to carrying out the Fowler recommendations in their entirety in this respect and bringing the C.B.C. as well as the private stations under the jurisdiction of the board of broadcast governors, thus removing that direct nexus which now exists between the management of the C.B.C. and the government, which did not exist under the old regime and which to my mind is entirely undesirable even if everybody behaves in the most proper manner possible. It seems to me that the insulation provided by the old board of the C.B.C. or the insulation of a board of broadcast governors between the government and the management of the C.B.C. was in the past a sound principle and should be restored. However, again I am expressing a view upon a matter which I think deserves further scrutiny by this committee.
Notwithstanding the fact that I feel I should perhaps go on speaking merely to

assert my right to debate these matters, I really feel I have said all that in principle I wanted to say. It seems to me this would be the most appropriate function of that committee even if there had been no undertaking in that regard, but in view of the undertaking I believe it should be carried out.
